title: 10 Flutter Performance Optimizations That Actually Matter
excerpt: Most Flutter optimization guides recycle the same 3 tips. Here are the ones I use in production — from widget rebuild analysis to isolate-based background processing.
content:
After building several production Flutter apps, I've learned that the gap between 'it works' and 'it works smoothly on a budget Android phone' is where real engineering happens. Here are the optimizations I reach for repeatedly.

1. const constructors everywhere

This sounds obvious, but I routinely audit PRs where const is missing from widgets that never change. A missing const means Flutter can't cache the widget instance, and it rebuilds on every frame.

2. RepaintBoundary at the right level

Wrapping your entire screen in a RepaintBoundary does nothing useful. The trick is identifying the smallest subtree that repaints independently. In practice, this means isolating animated components (like a typing indicator or progress bar) from static content.

3. ListView.builder with itemExtent when possible

If every item has the same height, set itemExtent. Flutter can calculate scroll positions without measuring every child, which matters enormously when you have thousands of items.

4. Avoid Opacity on heavy widgets

Wrapping a complex widget tree in Opacity tells Flutter to repaint the entire subtree even at opacity 0. Use Visibility or swap the widget out entirely when invisible.

5. Use Isolate for CPU-heavy work

JSON parsing 50,000 records on the main isolate freezes the UI for 2-3 seconds. I move deserialization to a separate isolate using compute() or Isolate.run(). The API surface is small but the impact is dramatic.

6. Cache network images properly

cached_network_image is not optional — it's table stakes. But also set maxWidthDiskCache and maxHeightDiskCache to match your UI, so you're not caching full-resolution images for 48px avatars.

7. Shader compilation warm-up

First-run jank is real. I ship a short animation on the splash screen that forces Flutter to compile shaders before the user interacts with the app. It's invisible to the user but eliminates early jank.

8. Use AnimatedBuilder instead of setState for animations

Calling setState 60 times per second rebuilds your entire widget. AnimatedBuilder isolates the rebuild to exactly what's animating.

9. Pre-split large widgets

A 500-line build method is a performance smell regardless of whether it causes measurable lag. Breaking it into smaller widgets with const constructors gives Flutter's diffing algorithm less work to do.

10. Profile, don't guess

Flutter DevTools has a timeline view. Use it. Every app's bottleneck is different — mine was a deeply nested CustomPainter in a financial chart. Yours might be something entirely different.

title: What I Learned Building a Production FastAPI Backend From Scratch
excerpt: Dependency injection, async database sessions, background tasks with Celery, and the mistakes I made structuring a real FastAPI project for a Japanese learning platform.
content:
I built a Japanese-language learning platform backend with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, and Celery. Here's what the official docs don't tell you about structuring a real project.

Project structure matters immediately

FastAPI's 'bigger applications' docs show a structure, but in practice you'll hit import cycle issues fast. I settled on: app/routers/, app/services/, app/models/, app/schemas/, with a deps.py file for reusable dependency callables.

Async database sessions are not plug-and-play

SQLAlchemy async with asyncpg works, but you need to be deliberate about session lifecycle. I use async with SessionLocal() as session: in a dependency, but the gotcha is that lazy-loaded relationships don't work in async mode — you must use selectinload() or joinedload() eagerly.

Background tasks: Celery vs ARQ vs FastAPI BackgroundTasks

BackgroundTasks is fine for in-process fire-and-forget (email, push notifications). But for anything that can fail and needs retry — data processing, content deduplication — I reached for Celery with Redis as the broker. The config is verbose but the retry semantics are battle-tested.

Dependency injection is FastAPI's superpower

Once you internalize that every route parameter with Depends() can be a full callable that accesses the database, current user, or any other service — you start writing dramatically cleaner code. My get_current_user dependency handles JWT validation, user lookup, and permission checks in one callable.

Testing: use TestClient with a real test database

Mocking the database is tempting but gives false confidence. I create a test database per pytest session, run Alembic migrations, and use dependency overrides to swap the production DB session for a test one. The setup is more work upfront, but it catches actual SQL bugs.

title: Bangladesh FinTech 2026: What's Actually Shipping
excerpt: Working inside a bank's ICT division gives a different perspective on FinTech than reading TechCrunch. Here's what's real, what's hype, and where the opportunities are.
content:
Bangladesh's FinTech conversation is dominated by MFS (bKash, Nagad) and agent banking. But working inside the ICT division of a scheduled bank, I see a different landscape — one that's less about consumer apps and more about infrastructure.

The real digital transformation is backend-first

Most banks are replacing core banking systems, not building flashy apps. The priority is API-first architecture for inter-bank settlement, real-time fraud detection, and regulatory reporting automation. If you can build systems that handle CBS migration without a single day of downtime, you're in demand.

Open banking is coming slower than the hype suggests

Bangladesh Bank's API guidelines exist on paper, but implementation is gradual. The technical challenge isn't the API design — it's data standardization across 61 scheduled banks, each with different core systems and data models.

Islamic finance tech is underinvested

Bangladesh has a significant Islamic banking sector, but the software ecosystem is thin. Zakat calculation engines, Shariah-compliant investment trackers, and Sukuk management platforms are all manual-heavy today. This is where I'm spending my R&D time.

The talent gap is real and specific

We don't have a shortage of Python or React developers. The gap is engineers who understand both banking domain logic AND modern software practices. Someone who can explain NPL provisioning rules AND write a FastAPI service with proper error handling — that combination is rare and valuable.
